title: Adulthood and Ageing
summary: Adulthood is marked by society's expectation that one performs the duties of an adult; family and career are the major milestones. In Indian tradition it is the Grihastha Ashram: entering social life and accepting responsibilities of family, marriage and career. Sub-periods: young adulthood (20s to 30s), middle adulthood (40s to 50s) and later adulthood (60s and above).

The person sees self as autonomous and independent and is less dependent financially on the parental family. Major tasks: choice of a career, starting family life, financial and emotional independence, close relationships with professional peers and community, concern for social issues. Typical crises: unemployment and marital discord. Erikson: crisis of intimacy versus isolation (ability to form deep relationships, particularly in marriage, or become isolated). A 'dream' of future accomplishment motivates goal-directed effort. In the early thirties people reappraise choices: the 'age thirty transition'.

Forties and fifties: competence, maturity, responsibility and stability; attention on health, children's future, ageing parents, leisure and plans for old age. Menopause occurs in women between 45 and 50; men worry about health, strength, power and sexual potency. It is a period of creativity (best works of scientists, writers and artists in late forties and early fifties). Erikson: generativity versus self-absorption. The middle-age transition is turbulent: awareness of mortality, taking stock of life, occupational changes, divorce, and coming to terms with retirement.

Later adulthood begins around sixty; people retire and fear for their health; common stereotypes say the elderly are inactive, intellectually declining, narrow-minded and religious; many lose spouses and feel insecure, but many remain healthy and active. Ageing is also psychological; Gandhi led the freedom struggle at 77; Baba Amte, Ramakrishna Paramhansa and Mother Teresa were achievers of late adulthood. Older people hold a reservoir of knowledge, experience and wisdom.

Body organs show a 0.8 to 1 per cent decline per year in functional ability after age 30 (partly normal, partly disease-related, partly caused by stress, nutrition, occupational status). External changes: graying hair, ageing skin, wrinkles, change of posture. Internal changes: respiratory, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular and central nervous systems. Sensory capacities slow down. Cognitive changes: memory, learning, attention and speed of performance are adversely affected; concentration and responsiveness fall; dementia and Alzheimer's disease are important diseases of old age. Key to a longer, healthier life: healthy diet, regular exercise, reduced stress, no smoking, alcohol or drugs, positive qualities, social welfare activities, spirituality and faith.
## Coping with problems of old age

Ageing can be delayed but not escaped; accept one's age and act realistically but optimistically; lead a disciplined life with rest, proper work habits, less tension, proper nutrition and spirituality. Coping strategies: flexibility, exploring new ways of coping, information seeking and problem solving rather than withdrawal, self-confidence and self-reliance, effective coping skills and an active approach. Social support: enlarging the social network, joining clubs, friends of one's own age for trusting relationships; grandparenting gives emotional satisfaction and role-model status.
## Importance of the aged in society

The Indian multigenerational structure (joint family) values elders as repositories of knowledge and experience; a Sanskrit verse says those who greet and serve elders grow in longevity, knowledge, fame and strength. The nuclear family system deprives children of cultural transmission (stories, morals), affecting their emotional expression and values; many social problems stem from the breakdown of the family system.

sa: Describe the characteristics of young adulthood.

Autonomy and independence, financial independence from parents, choice of career, starting a family, close peer relationships, concern for society; unemployment and marital discord are crises and intimacy versus isolation is the Erikson crisis.
Describe the characteristics of middle adulthood.

Competence, maturity, responsibility and stability; attention on health, children and ageing parents and plans for old age; menopause in women; creativity; generativity versus self-absorption; turbulence from awareness of mortality.
Explain the physical changes in ageing.

Organs decline by 0.8–1 per cent per year after 30; external changes are graying hair, wrinkles and posture changes; internal changes are in respiratory, digestive, cardiovascular and nervous systems; sensory abilities slow down.
Explain the cognitive changes in ageing.
Memory, learning, attention and speed of performance decline, concentration and responsiveness decrease and dementia and Alzheimer's occur; older people also become more vulnerable.
How can one cope with the problems of old age?

Accept one's age realistically and optimistically, be flexible, explore new coping methods, solve problems instead of withdrawing, build self-confidence, lead a disciplined life and use social support.
Why are aged people important to society?
They hold knowledge, experience and wisdom, transmit culture to the young, and the joint family with elders supports multi-dimensional growth.
la: Describe young, middle and old adulthood.

Young adulthood (20s–30s): career, family, independence, intimacy versus isolation, age thirty transition. Middle adulthood (40s–50s): competence, stability, menopause, creativity, generativity versus self-absorption, turbulence and retirement planning. Old age (60+): retirement, health concerns, stereotypes, yet many remain active, with a store of wisdom.
Discuss physical and cognitive changes during adulthood and old age and the key to healthy life.

Organs decline 0.8–1 per cent a year after 30; external changes (gray hair, wrinkles), internal changes (organ systems) and sensory slowing occur; memory, learning, attention and speed decline, with dementia and Alzheimer's. A healthy diet, exercise, less stress, no smoking or alcohol, social welfare and spirituality help.
Explain how people can cope with the problems of old age and the role of social support.

Accept one's age, lead a disciplined life, be flexible, seek information and solve problems, build self-confidence and self-reliance. Social networks, clubs and friends give emotional expression and trust; grandparenting gives role-model status and satisfaction.
Discuss the importance of the aged in society and the effect of breakdown of the family system.

Elders are repositories of knowledge and cultural transmission; the joint family supports growth in longevity, knowledge, fame and strength. The shift to nuclear families deprives children of stories and morals, affecting values and emotional expression and causing social problems.
